catalog_locator: p. 187, section 4.2 Schwa deletion; p. 192-193, section 6 Tone; p. 198, section 7 Conclusion
catalog_quote: A schwa can be deleted in a fast speech in the language, example, /kə̄lú/ → [klú] ‘earlier’, and /kə̄rám/ → [krám] ‘to plan’. This schwa deletion seems to be occurring on a sesquisyllable, a prominent feature in Tibeto-Burman languages (Matisoff: 1973). This kind of syllable is a bi-syllabic word which has an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed syllable. These unstressed syllables are usually a prefix followed by the main root: prefix+root- as in kə̄-réŋ ‘garden’. It may be noted that there are other words too which are not in the form of prefix+root, that means to say, a given bi-syllable itself is a root morpheme, but still allows a schwa deletion, example, /məwi/ → [mui] ‘grow’, and /kə̄río/ → [krío] ‘insert’. [p. 187] ... There are four lexical tone contrasting as high, mid, low and extra low in Liangmai and this has been observed in all varieties of Liangmai that I have studied so far. [p. 192] ... A syllable in Liangmai is considered as a tone bearing unit (TBU) rather than a vowel or a rhyme. [p. 193] ... A prosodic features such as stress, rhythm and intonation patterns will be an important feature to study in future. [p. 198]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Liangmai is a tone language (four contrastive level tones; the syllable is the tone-bearing unit). The only stress claim is that in sesquisyllabic disyllables (typically prefix + root, e.g. kə̄-réŋ 'garden') the first, prefix syllable is unstressed and the root syllable that follows is stressed, which licenses schwa deletion in fast speech. No general word-stress rule is given; the author explicitly leaves stress, rhythm and intonation for future study.
new_statements.exceptions: Schwa deletion also applies to bisyllabic root morphemes that are not prefix+root (/məwi/ → [mui] 'grow', /kə̄río/ → [krío] 'insert'); the stress characterisation is not explicitly extended to these.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, restricted to sesquisyllabic (prefix+root) disyllables; observed via fast-speech schwa deletion. Author's data mainly from the North Eastern Liangmai area but claims to cover all varieties studied.
new_statements.identity_note: Mataina 2022 describes Liangmai (lian1251) generally, drawing mainly on the North Eastern Liangmai area (author's Maguilong village) but claiming the tone facts for all varieties he has studied; he groups Liangmai villages into five dialect areas (North Eastern, Central, South Eastern, South Western, Nagaland/Ntu). No separate Glottolog dialect codes are involved. The earlier theses each describe a village variety (Widinibou 2011: Kabangning/North Eastern; Daimai G. 2016: Thalon/South Western; Raguibou 2015: Namtiram/South Western).

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Mataina 2022 statement: a tone language in which the sesquisyllabic minor (prefixal schwa) syllable is unstressed/reduced relative to the following root syllable, shown by schwa deletion. Adds nothing on placement beyond that; tone count differs (three here vs four in Mataina 2022) but that is not a stress matter. The work is comparative (Zeme, Liangmai, Rongmei); the quoted Liangmai section and examples are specifically Liangmai.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Liangmai is tonal (three contrastive tones, syllable template (C1)V1(V2)(C2)T). The only stress-related remark is indirect: the schwa of a prefixal/minor first syllable is 'unstressed or reduced' and drops in casual speech to give an initial obstruent+liquid cluster (/pəlam/ > /plam/), i.e. the reduced minor syllable precedes the full (tone-bearing) root syllable. No stress-placement rule, no statement on stress being contrastive or absent.
new_statements.exceptions: cluster formation limited to obstruent + liquid (/p t k/ + /r l/), casual/spontaneous speech
new_statements.identity_note: All three theses describe Liangmai (Liangmai Naga, lian1251; Zeliangrong group) as spoken in Tamenglong/Senapati districts of Manipur and Peren district of Nagaland; Daimai 2016 notes village-to-village variation without fixing a reference dialect. Raguibou 2015 is comparative (Zeme, Liangmai, Rongmei); only its Liangmai sections (§3.2, Liangmai rows of ch. 4-5) were used here.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement about stress: none of the three theses has a stress/accent section or a stress-placement rule; all three call Liangmai a tone language. The only stress-relevant content is Raguibou 2015's remark (pp. 120-121) that the 'unstressed or reduced' schwa of a prefixal first syllable drops in casual speech (/pəlam/ > /plam/), which matches the existing Mataina 2022 statement (sesquisyllable = unstressed prefix syllable + stressed root syllable). The sources do disagree on the tone inventory (Widinibou 2011: three contour tones rising/level/falling; Daimai 2016 and Raguibou 2015: three level tones high/mid/low; Mataina 2022: four tones), and Widinibou 2011 reports, without adopting it, an amateur source's 'stress tone' as a fourth tone; neither point bears on word-stress placement.
